title: Kv3 channel expression predicted shorter spikes in 182 mouse brain regions beyond spatial and random-gene nulls, but T-type calcium-channel expression did not predict bursts (IBL, Allen MERFISH)
abstract: Question: do the ion-channel genes that set spike features in single cells predict the same features across mouse brain regions? Earlier work found that input wiring and cell-type mix both predict regional spiking, and that cortical input share S predicts thalamic bursts. Data: spike phenotypes of 62,049 IBL Brain-Wide Map units in 182 regions; burst fraction in 27 thalamic nuclei; region expression of 14,377 genes from Allen MERFISH neurons (1.92 million, one brain; 0.99 million, a second brain) with 10x cluster-mean expression. The plan was frozen before analysis. Nulls: 1,000 spatial surrogate maps and 10,000 random gene sets. Results: the Kv3 index (Kcnc1-3) correlated with spike duration at rho -0.61 (surrogate p = 0.001; gene-set p = 0.007), and at -0.30 inside brain divisions (gene-set p = 0.0008). It replicated in the second MERFISH brain (-0.54) and in 26 Allen Visual Coding regions (-0.69). Pvalb predicted the narrow-unit fraction better than Kv3 (rho 0.61 vs 0.45), so that hypothesis failed. Cacna1g (Cav3.1) did not predict brain-wide burstiness (rho 0.12, p = 0.29) or thalamic burst fraction (0.37, p = 0.059). S kept partial rho 0.77 given Cacna1g, but not given midline position or a few genes of the medial-lateral thalamic axis. Removing Kv3 halved the link between input similarity and duration similarity (beta 0.43 to 0.20, still p = 0.041); removing Pvalb made it non-significant, but many genes also reduced it. Limitations: correlational, region averages, cluster-mean expression, extracellular unit bias; the gene null cannot separate Kv3 from co-expressed fast-spiking markers.
